title: Contracts & Instruments
hook: MNQ isn't just a ticker on your screen. Know what you're actually trading.

launchpad.outcome: Name the common futures instruments and explain the difference between a mini and a micro contract.
launchpad.missionQuestion: If someone switches from 1 MNQ contract to 1 NQ contract, does their risk stay the same?

seeIt.heading: Meet the instrument pairs
seeIt.prompt: Each of these has a mini and a micro version. Watch them build up.

cards.label: MNQ ↔ NQ
cards.text: Micro E-mini Nasdaq-100 and E-mini Nasdaq-100. Same underlying index family — MNQ is 1/10 the contract multiplier of NQ.

cards.label: MES ↔ ES
cards.text: Micro E-mini S&P 500 and E-mini S&P 500. Same relationship — the micro is the smaller-dollar-risk version.

cards.label: MGC ↔ GC
cards.text: Micro Gold and Gold. Metals work the same way — a micro and a mini version of the same underlying market.

cards.label: The takeaway
cards.text: A futures contract's value moves with its underlying market — it isn't ownership. Contract specs differ by instrument, so always verify current exchange specs before trading.

rounds.question: Which pair correctly matches the instrument to its name?

options.label: MGC → Micro Gold
options.why: MGC is Micro Gold. ES is the full-size E-mini S&P 500 (MES is the micro), and MNQ is the micro version of NQ.

options.label: ES → Micro E-mini S&P 500
options.feedback: ES is the full-size E-mini S&P 500 — MES is the micro version.

options.label: MNQ → E-mini Nasdaq-100
options.feedback: MNQ is the MICRO E-mini Nasdaq-100 — NQ is the full-size version.

rounds.question: A trader switches from trading 1 contract of MNQ to 5 contracts of MNQ. Has she changed instruments?

options.label: No — she's still trading MNQ; only her size and dollar exposure changed
options.why: The instrument stays MNQ — contract count only changes exposure.

options.label: Yes — 5 contracts makes it a different instrument
options.feedback: Contract count never changes what instrument you're trading.

options.label: It's impossible to tell without knowing the price
options.feedback: Price doesn't determine the instrument either — she's still trading MNQ either way.

rounds.scenario: A trader moves from MNQ to NQ but keeps the same number of contracts because "the chart looks the same."
rounds.question: What's wrong with that reasoning?

options.label: The contract multiplier is different, so the same price move produces very different P&L and risk
options.why: Exactly — the chart shape being similar doesn't mean the dollar exposure is similar.

options.label: Nothing — NQ and MNQ are the same size, just different tickers
options.feedback: They're not the same size — MNQ is 1/10 the contract multiplier of NQ.

sayItBack.prompt: Imagine another AGHF girl asks: "What's actually different between MNQ and NQ?" How would you explain it to her?
sayItBack.modelAnswer: They're the same underlying market — the Nasdaq-100 — just different contract sizes. MNQ is the micro version, worth 1/10 of what NQ is per point. So the exact same price move on the exact same chart means very different dollar risk depending on which one you're actually trading. The chart looks identical either way — the instrument is what determines how much money is on the line.

checklist: A futures contract's value moves with its underlying market — it isn't ownership.
Micro contracts (MNQ, MES, MGC) are a fraction of their mini counterparts (NQ, ES, GC).
Contract count changes your exposure, not the instrument itself.
Know the instrument. Know its value. Know your risk.

takeaways: A futures contract's value moves with its underlying market — it isn't ownership.
Micro contracts (MNQ, MES, MGC) are a fraction of their mini counterparts (NQ, ES, GC).
Contract count changes your exposure, not the instrument itself.
remember: Know the instrument. Know its value. Know your risk.
